analogy.p: A vaccine is like a **fire drill**: the alarm sounds, everyone practises where to go and who does what, but there is no real fire. The staff (white blood cells) learn the plan and a few people (memory cells) are trained as fire wardens who stay for years. When a real fire (the pathogen) starts, the building is evacuated and the fire is dealt with in minutes rather than hours, so there is little damage (no illness). Herd immunity is like a building where nearly everyone knows the drill, so a small fire cannot spread. The analogy breaks down because a fire drill is the same every time, whereas the immune system makes **specific antibodies** for each pathogen and a new drill (vaccine) is needed if the pathogen mutates.
analogy.t: Fire drill for the immune system

bullets: Spec key phrase: **'dead or inactive forms of a pathogen'** are introduced in **'small quantities'**.
The white blood cells are **stimulated to produce antibodies** specific to the pathogen's antigens.
On later exposure the response is **quicker** (and larger), so the person does not develop the disease.
Vaccination **protects individuals** in the future and, if enough people are immune, **reduces the spread** of the pathogen through the population.
You must be able to **evaluate** vaccination: benefits against risks, ethical issues and practical problems.
Vaccination is a **preventative** measure; it is not a treatment for someone who is already ill.
Link: this builds on **how the body defends itself against pathogens** (phagocytosis, antibodies, antitoxins) and leads on to **antibiotics, drug development and monoclonal antibodies**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1.7 (Vaccination) expects you to **describe how vaccination works**, **explain how it protects an individual** and **explain how it protects a population (herd immunity)**. The spec wording is that vaccination involves introducing **small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen** into the body to **stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies**. If the same pathogen enters later, the white blood cells **respond quickly** to produce the correct antibodies, **preventing infection**. You also need to be able to **evaluate the global use of vaccination** in the prevention of disease. It matters because vaccination is the single most effective way of preventing many infectious diseases, and the reasoning chain (antigen, antibody, memory cell, faster response) is a guaranteed source of marks.

bullets: **Antigen** = a molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a cell or pathogen that triggers an immune response.
**Antibody** = a protein made by lymphocytes with a shape **complementary to one specific antigen**.
Antibodies are **specific**: antibodies against measles will not work against mumps because the antigens have different shapes.
Antibodies bind to antigens and **mark the pathogen for destruction** by phagocytes; they can also cause pathogens to clump together.
The first time a pathogen is met, it takes the lymphocytes **several days** to find the right antibody and make enough of it.
During that delay the pathogen reproduces rapidly, so the person **gets symptoms** (the disease).
Other white blood cell responses you should know are **phagocytosis** (engulfing pathogens) and **antitoxin production** (neutralising toxins); vaccination mainly uses the **antibody** route.
Link to non-specific defences: skin, mucus, stomach acid, hairs and cilia, and tears/lysozyme are the **first line** and do not depend on antigens.
core.h: Revision of the immune response: antigens and antibodies
core.p: Every pathogen (bacterium, virus, fungus or protist) has **antigens** on its surface. Antigens are **molecules, usually proteins, that are recognised by the immune system as foreign**. When a pathogen gets into the body, **white blood cells called lymphocytes** detect its antigens and respond by producing **antibodies**. An antibody is a **protein with a specific shape** that fits (is **complementary** to) the antigen on one particular pathogen. Antibodies lock onto the pathogen, **clump pathogens together (agglutination)** and mark them so that **phagocytes** engulf and digest them. This takes time the first time a pathogen is met, which is why you can become ill before the body wins.

bullets: Contains **dead, inactive or weakened** pathogens, or fragments carrying **the pathogen's antigens**.
Antigens are **the same shape** as those on the live pathogen, so they trigger the **same antibody response**.
Dead or inactive pathogens **cannot cause the disease**, so the vaccine is generally safe.
Given by **injection** (most vaccines) or sometimes by mouth or nasal spray, depending on the vaccine.
Only **small quantities** are needed because the immune system multiplies the response itself.
Each vaccine is **specific to one pathogen** (or a combined one such as MMR, which contains three).
Some vaccines contain a substance called an **adjuvant** that boosts the immune response (not required by the spec).
Vaccines **do not contain the antibodies themselves**; they contain antigens so that the body makes its own antibodies.
core.p: A **vaccine** is a preparation that contains **antigens from a pathogen in a harmless form**, so the immune system can learn to recognise the pathogen **without the person catching the disease**. In the AQA specification the pathogen is present as **dead or inactive** forms, in **small quantities**. The antigens on the dead or inactive pathogen are the same shape as those on the live, dangerous one, so the lymphocytes treat them as the real thing. Because the pathogen cannot reproduce (or cannot cause disease), the person is **not made ill** by the vaccine itself, though mild symptoms can occur.

bullets: **Step 1:** vaccine (dead or inactive pathogen with antigens) is injected into the body.
**Step 2:** the antigens are recognised as foreign by **white blood cells (lymphocytes)**.
**Step 3:** the lymphocytes are stimulated to **produce antibodies** that are complementary to the antigens.
**Step 4:** the antibodies bind to the antigens, and the harmless pathogen is destroyed (e.g. by phagocytes).
**Step 5:** some lymphocytes become **memory cells** that remain in the blood and can respond again.
This first response is called the **primary response**: it is **slow** (days) and produces a **small** amount of antibody.
The person usually feels **no or very mild symptoms**, because the vaccine pathogen is harmless.
Link: lymphocytes dividing by mitosis uses the **cell cycle** knowledge from cell biology.
core.h: How vaccination works: step by step (the primary response)
core.p: The sequence of events is worth learning as a chain, because 4 and 6-mark questions reward each link. First the vaccine is injected, introducing the harmless antigens. **Lymphocytes with receptors that fit those antigens** detect them and become activated. The activated lymphocytes **divide by mitosis** to produce a large number of cells, some of which become **plasma cells that secrete antibodies** into the blood. Antibody concentration rises, peaks and then **falls** as the antigens are cleared. Importantly, a few of the lymphocytes become **memory cells**, which stay in the body for years. The person has not been ill, but their immune system has been 'trained'.

bullets: **Primary response:** slow, small peak of antibody, may take **about 1 to 2 weeks** to peak.
**Secondary response:** **faster** (starts within days or even hours), **much higher** peak, and antibodies **stay at a high level for longer**.
The difference is due to **memory cells**, which are already 'primed' to recognise the antigen.
The pathogen is destroyed **before symptoms develop**: the person is **immune** to that disease.
Immunity may last **years or a lifetime**, or fade (so **booster** doses are used for some vaccines).
Memory cells are specific: they only respond to **the antigens of that one pathogen** (or very similar strains).
Exam phrase: 'memory cells **quickly** produce the **correct antibodies** in **larger amounts**, so the pathogen is **destroyed before it can cause illness**'.
Never say that the body 'remembers the disease'; say that **memory cells** remember the **antigen**.
core.h: Memory cells and the secondary response
core.p: The key to protection is the **memory cell**. If the **same pathogen** (with the same antigens) enters the body later, memory cells recognise the antigens **immediately**. They divide rapidly and produce plasma cells, so the body makes **the correct antibodies much more quickly and in much larger amounts** than the first time. This is the **secondary response**. Because the antibody level rises so fast, the real pathogen is destroyed **before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms**, and the person does not become ill. This is what the spec means by 'the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection'.

bullets: Antibodies fit **one antigen shape** (like a key fits one lock), so protection is **specific**.
**Mutation** of the pathogen's genes can change the antigen, so memory cells **no longer recognise** it.
The **flu vaccine** is updated **every year** to match the strains predicted to spread.
Pathogens that mutate quickly (flu, HIV, the common cold) are **hard to vaccinate against** for lasting protection.
Vaccines that cover **several pathogens** (e.g. **MMR** for measles, mumps, rubella) contain antigens from each one.
Link to **evolution**: a strain with a new antigen that escapes immunity has a **survival advantage** and spreads by natural selection.
A vaccine given **too late**, after infection has begun, will be too slow to help, because the primary response takes days.
core.h: Why one vaccine does not protect against everything
core.p: Because antibodies and memory cells are **specific** to particular antigens, a vaccine gives protection only against the **pathogen (or strain) it was made from**. A measles vaccine does nothing against mumps, and a vaccine against one type of influenza virus may not work against another. Some pathogens, such as the **influenza virus**, **mutate frequently**, which changes the shape of their antigens. Memory cells for the old antigen no longer fit the new one, so a **new vaccine has to be produced each year** for the strains expected to be circulating. This is also why the common cold, caused by many different viruses, has no single vaccine.

bullets: Herd immunity = when enough of a population is **immune** that the pathogen cannot spread easily, **even to unvaccinated people**.
The more infectious the disease, the **higher the percentage** that needs to be vaccinated (measles about 95 percent).
Protects **babies, elderly people, pregnant women and those with weak immune systems** who cannot be vaccinated or respond poorly.
If vaccination rates **fall** (for example because of unfounded health scares), herd immunity is lost and **outbreaks return**.
A pathogen can be **eradicated** if vaccination is global and sustained: **smallpox** was declared eradicated in 1980.
**Polio** has been eliminated from many countries thanks to vaccination programmes.
In diagrams, immune people are shown as a **barrier** that stops the infection passing to the few unprotected people.
Do not say herd immunity means 'everyone is immune'; it means **enough** people are immune to stop the spread.
core.p: If a **large proportion of the population is immune** to a pathogen, the spread of that pathogen is **very much reduced**. This is called **herd (community) immunity**. It happens because most people that an infected person meets are immune, so the pathogen **has few susceptible hosts to infect** and the chain of transmission is broken. Herd immunity **protects people who cannot be vaccinated**, such as **babies too young for the vaccine**, people with **weakened immune systems** (for example during chemotherapy) and those who have had a **severe reaction** to a vaccine. The proportion needed depends on how easily the pathogen spreads: for highly infectious **measles** it is around **95 percent**.

bullets: **MMR:** one combined vaccine against **measles, mumps and rubella**; given in two doses in childhood.
**Measles** can cause serious complications such as pneumonia, brain swelling and death; it spreads through **droplets** from coughs and sneezes.
**HPV vaccine:** protects against the virus that is the main cause of **cervical cancer**, a good example of vaccination preventing a non-communicable outcome.
**Seasonal flu vaccine:** reformulated each year; offered to the elderly, young children and people with health conditions.
**Boosters:** extra doses that restart the memory cell response when immunity might be fading.
**Smallpox** was eradicated worldwide by 1980 following a global vaccination campaign.
**Travel vaccines** (for example for typhoid or yellow fever) protect individuals going to areas where the disease is common.
Programmes need **record-keeping, storage (cold chain), trained staff and public trust** to succeed.
core.p: Governments run **vaccination programmes** that offer vaccines at set ages, with **booster** doses when needed. In the UK children are offered vaccines such as **MMR** (measles, mumps and rubella), **polio**, **whooping cough (pertussis)**, **HPV** for human papillomavirus (which can cause cervical cancer) and **seasonal flu** for vulnerable groups. The success of a programme depends on a **high uptake** in the population. Large-scale vaccination has made once-common diseases rare in many countries, and it is the reason why you are unlikely to meet diseases like measles or polio in the UK today.

bullets: **Prevents the disease** before it starts, so there is no suffering and no complications such as brain damage, infertility or death.
Provides **long-lasting protection** (years or a lifetime) in many cases.
Produces **herd immunity**, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
**Eradication** is possible (smallpox), saving millions of lives and no further need for vaccination against that disease.
**Cost-effective:** preventing disease costs less than treating it and avoids time off work and school.
Works against **viruses** where antibiotics cannot help.
Reduces the spread of **antibiotic-resistant bacteria** because fewer infections mean fewer antibiotics are used.
Protects against some **cancers** (HPV vaccine and cervical cancer).
core.p: When you evaluate vaccination you must weigh up benefits and risks. The benefits are very large. Vaccination **prevents illness and death**, protects **both the individual and the community**, and costs far less than treating the disease. It has led to the **eradication of smallpox** and the near eradication of polio. Because there are fewer cases, **fewer people need hospital treatment**, which saves money and frees NHS resources. Vaccination can also protect people against diseases that **have no cure** (viral diseases cannot be treated with antibiotics), making prevention the best option.

bullets: **Mild side effects** are common: soreness, redness, fever; severe allergic reactions are **very rare**.
A vaccine is **not 100 percent effective**; a small number of vaccinated people may still catch the disease (usually more mildly).
Some vaccines require **several doses** or **boosters**, which costs money and needs people to attend.
**Cost and logistics:** vaccines often need to be stored **refrigerated** (the cold chain), which is difficult in remote or poor regions.
**Mutating pathogens** (flu, HIV) need new vaccines or are hard to vaccinate against.
**Ethical debate:** individual choice against protecting the community; some people refuse vaccination for **religious, personal or misinformation** reasons.
A false link between **MMR and autism** (a discredited claim) caused vaccination rates to fall and **measles outbreaks** to return, which shows how important public trust is.
Always give a **balanced conclusion**: the benefits to individuals and society **greatly outweigh** the small risks for most vaccines.
core.p: No medical treatment is perfectly safe, and a balanced evaluation must include the drawbacks. Most side effects are **mild**, such as a **sore arm, a slight fever or feeling tired**, and they happen because the immune system is responding. **Severe reactions are very rare**, and the risk from the disease is nearly always far greater than the risk from the vaccine. Other limitations are practical: some vaccines **do not give 100 percent protection**, some need **boosters**, pathogens that mutate quickly need **new vaccines**, and in poorer countries **cost, storage and access** are barriers. Some people object on **personal or religious grounds**, or are influenced by false information.

bullets: **Vaccine:** given **before** infection; uses **antigens**; protects through **memory cells**; effective against **viruses and bacteria**.
**Antibiotic:** given **during** infection; a chemical; kills **bacteria only**; does not give lasting immunity.
**Painkillers** only relieve symptoms; they do not kill pathogens (see the next point on drugs).
A vaccine does **not** contain antibodies; **antibodies** given directly (as in some emergency treatments) give only short-term protection.
Immunity from vaccination is **active immunity** because the body makes its own antibodies (the terms are not required by the spec).
**Prevention is better than cure:** vaccinating reduces cases, deaths and healthcare costs.
If a person is already infected, a vaccine will usually be **too slow** to help.
core.h: Vaccination compared with antibiotics and treatment
core.p: It is easy to confuse vaccines with medicines, but they work in completely different ways. **Vaccination prevents** a disease by training the immune system **before** infection. **Antibiotics treat** a bacterial infection **after** it has started by killing bacteria or stopping their growth. Antibiotics have **no effect on viruses**, while vaccines can protect against **both viral and bacterial** diseases. A vaccine produces **long-term** protection through memory cells, while an antibiotic works only while it is in the body. Using vaccination reduces the need for antibiotics and helps slow the development of **antibiotic resistance**.

bullets: Describe the **time delay** before antibody appears (lag) for each exposure.
Compare the **peak height** using figures: say how many times higher the second peak is (divide the values).
Compare the **time to reach the peak** (subtract the day numbers).
Explain: the second response is quicker and larger because **memory cells** were produced during the first exposure.
If the graph shows the person becoming ill after first exposure but not the second, link the **quick antibody production** to destroying the pathogen **before symptoms**.
State the **units** (arbitrary units, days) when quoting values.
Do not just say 'it goes up'; give a **specific comparison**, e.g. '160 units compared with 20 units'.
core.p: A very common exam question gives a graph of **antibody concentration against time** after one or two exposures to an antigen. The shape tells the whole story. After the first exposure there is a **delay (lag)** before any antibody appears, then a **slow rise to a small peak** and then a fall. After the second exposure the line **rises much sooner, much more steeply and to a much higher peak**, and stays high for longer. Describe the graph using numbers from the axes, read carefully with units, and always explain the difference using **memory cells**.

bullets: **Percentage vaccinated** = (number vaccinated / total population) x 100.
**Number needed for a target** = target percentage / 100 x population, then subtract those already vaccinated.
**Percentage reduction** = (old value - new value) / old value x 100.
**Example:** 17 000 of 20 000 vaccinated is 17 000 / 20 000 x 100 = **85 percent**.
To reach 95 percent of 20 000 you need 19 000; so **2 000 more** people must be vaccinated.
Cases fall from 240 to 36: reduction = (240 - 36) / 240 x 100 = **85 percent**.
In graphs of cases over time, describe the **trend before and after** the programme started, quoting data.
core.h: Calculations and maths skills with vaccination data
core.p: Vaccination questions often include simple maths with **percentages**, **ratios** and **rates**. You may be asked for the percentage of a population vaccinated, how many more people need vaccinating to reach a target, or the percentage reduction in cases after a programme. Show your working clearly: write the formula, substitute, and give the answer with a unit or percentage sign. Round sensibly and check that your answer is reasonable (a percentage of a population cannot exceed 100).

bullets: Link to **antibiotics and resistance**: fewer infections means less antibiotic use.
Link to **monoclonal antibodies** (triple): antibodies can be produced in the lab for diagnosis and treatment.
Link to **plant disease**: plants cannot be vaccinated, they rely on physical and chemical defences.
Link to **mutation and natural selection**: new flu strains arise and spread.
Link to **public health**: screening, hygiene and vaccination together control disease.
In 6-mark questions, finish with a **conclusion** that weighs benefit against risk.
Use precise words: **antigen, antibody, memory cell, white blood cell, immune, pathogen, herd immunity**.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: Vaccination ties together a lot of the infection and response topic and makes a good extended answer. It links to **communicable disease** (how pathogens spread and how spread is reduced), to **cell biology** (mitosis of lymphocytes), to **proteins and enzymes** (specific shapes, complementary fit), to **evolution** (mutation and new strains), and to **ethics in science**. When writing a longer answer, plan it as: what a vaccine contains, how the body responds the first time, what memory cells do on re-exposure, how that prevents disease, then herd immunity, then a balanced evaluation.

exam: **Describe how vaccination works (2 to 4 marks):** dead or inactive pathogen with antigens is injected (1); white blood cells recognise the antigens and produce antibodies (1); memory cells are produced (1); on re-infection the antibodies are produced faster and in larger amounts, so the person does not become ill (1).
**Explain why a person does not get ill after vaccination (3 marks):** memory cells remain, they quickly produce the correct antibodies, so the pathogen is destroyed before it can cause disease.
**Use exact spec words:** 'dead or inactive pathogen', 'white blood cells', 'antibodies', 'memory cells', 'quickly', 'correct antibodies'. Avoid 'the body gets used to it' or 'germs'.
**Herd immunity (2 marks):** a large proportion of the population is immune (1), so the spread of the pathogen is reduced and unvaccinated people are protected (1).
**Graph questions (3 to 4 marks):** quote values with units for lag time and peak height for both exposures, make a comparison (e.g. 8 times higher, 9 days faster), then explain with memory cells.
**Why a new flu vaccine every year (2 marks):** the virus mutates (1), changing its antigens so the memory cells/antibodies no longer fit (1).

**Evaluate global use of vaccination (6 marks):** benefits (prevents disease and death, herd immunity, eradication of smallpox, cost-effective), risks and limitations (mild side effects, rare severe reactions, not 100 percent effective, cost and storage, mutating pathogens, ethical objections), then a judged conclusion.
**Calculations (2 to 3 marks):** write the formula, substitute, give a percentage; for percentage reduction use (old - new) / old x 100.
**Command words:** 'describe' = steps in order; 'explain' = give reasons using because/so; 'evaluate' = both sides and a justified conclusion; 'suggest' = apply knowledge to a new case.
**Distinguish vaccines from antibiotics** when a question gives both: vaccines prevent (all pathogen types), antibiotics treat (bacteria only).
**Always link cause and effect:** vaccine, antigens, antibodies, memory cells, faster response, no illness.

mistakes.r: A vaccine contains dead or inactive pathogens (antigens); the body makes its own antibodies in response.
mistakes.w: A vaccine contains antibodies to fight the disease.

mistakes.r: The pathogen is dead or inactive, so it cannot cause the disease; it only stimulates white blood cells to produce antibodies.
mistakes.w: The vaccine gives you a small dose of the disease so you get the disease.

mistakes.r: Memory cells remain in the blood and, on re-exposure, quickly produce the correct antibodies in larger amounts.
mistakes.w: Memory cells fight the pathogen themselves / the body remembers the disease.

mistakes.r: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections that have started and do not give lasting protection; vaccines prevent infection.
mistakes.w: Antibiotics protect you from future infections like vaccines.

mistakes.r: Herd immunity means a large proportion is immune, so the spread of the pathogen is very much reduced and unvaccinated people are protected.
mistakes.w: Herd immunity means everyone in the population is vaccinated.

mistakes.r: Antibodies are specific to antigens; mutated strains (e.g. flu) have different antigens so new vaccines are needed.
mistakes.w: Vaccines work on any strain of the pathogen forever.

mistakes.r: Vaccination is preventative; the primary response is too slow to help someone already infected.
mistakes.w: Vaccination cures a person who is already ill.

mistakes.r: Side effects are usually mild and severe reactions are very rare; no vaccine is 100 percent effective but benefits greatly outweigh risks.
mistakes.w: Vaccines are 100 percent safe/100 percent effective, or are too dangerous to use.

mistakes.r: It is bigger and faster because memory cells from the first exposure are already primed to produce the correct antibodies.
mistakes.w: The second response is bigger because the pathogen is stronger.

summary: AQA 4.3.1.7: you must explain that a vaccine introduces small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen so that white blood cells produce antibodies and memory cells; if the pathogen enters again the response is quick, preventing infection, and if enough people are immune the spread of the pathogen is greatly reduced (herd immunity). You must also evaluate the global use of vaccination. It is a guaranteed source of marks in infection and response questions.

terms.d: Introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.
A preparation containing dead or inactive pathogens (or their antigens) used in vaccination.
A molecule, usually a protein, on the surface of a pathogen that is recognised as foreign by white blood cells and triggers an immune response.
A protein produced by white blood cells, with a shape complementary to a specific antigen, that binds to the pathogen and helps destroy it.
A cell of the immune system that recognises antigens and produces antibodies.
A white blood cell that remains in the body after an infection or vaccination and can quickly produce the correct antibodies if the same pathogen enters again.
The slow, small antibody response when a pathogen's antigens are first encountered.
The faster and larger antibody response on re-exposure to the same antigen, caused by memory cells.
Protected against a disease because the body can respond quickly with the correct antibodies.
Protection of a population from a pathogen when a large proportion of people are immune, so that its spread is very much reduced.
An additional dose of a vaccine given later to maintain a high level of memory cells.
A combined vaccine that protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
The complete removal of a disease from the world, as achieved for smallpox in 1980.
A change in the genetic material of an organism, which can change the shape of antigens so that memory cells no longer recognise the pathogen.
The engulfing and digestion of pathogens by phagocytes (a type of white blood cell).
Used to stop a disease happening in the first place, rather than to treat it.

worked.ans: Model answer: The vaccine contains a dead or inactive form of the pathogen with its antigens. White blood cells detect the antigens and produce antibodies, and some become memory cells. If the live pathogen enters later, the memory cells quickly produce the correct antibodies in larger amounts, so the pathogen is destroyed before it can cause illness.
worked.q: Explain how a vaccination protects a person from a disease in the future. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: the vaccine contains dead or inactive (harmless) pathogen with antigens.
Mark 2: white blood cells recognise the antigens and produce antibodies; memory cells are formed.
Mark 3: if the same pathogen enters later, the memory cells respond quickly.
Mark 4: the correct antibodies are produced faster and in larger amounts, so the pathogen is destroyed before it causes the disease.

worked.ans: The second response was faster (peak after 5 days compared with 14 days) and larger (160 units compared with 20 units, 8 times higher). This is because memory cells made after the first injection quickly produced the correct antibodies in large amounts.
worked.q: After a first injection, antibody concentration first rose above zero at day 7 and peaked at 20 units on day 14. After a second injection at day 60, it first rose at day 62 and peaked at 160 units on day 65. Compare the two responses and explain the difference. (4 marks)
steps: Peak height: 160 / 20 = 8 times higher after the second injection.
Time to peak: first = 14 days; second = 65 - 60 = 5 days, so 9 days quicker.
Lag: first = 7 days; second = 2 days after injection.
Explanation: memory cells formed after the first injection respond quickly to the antigen.

worked.q: A town of 20 000 people has 17 000 vaccinated against measles. Herd immunity needs 95 percent vaccinated. (a) Calculate the percentage vaccinated. (b) How many more people must be vaccinated? (c) Cases fell from 240 to 36 after the programme began; calculate the percentage reduction. (5 marks)
